verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, on Jeduthun. A psalm, of David.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster, to be sung in the manner of Jeduthun: a psalm of David.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the heading, and the Hebrew counts it as verse 1, which is why the KJV's numbers are all one behind. The headings of the psalms were instructions to performers, the nearest thing the ancient world has to a stage direction. 'The choirmaster' (lamnatzeach) is the one who leads the singing. The phrase 'al yedutun is the sort of line the KJV tidies into 'to Jeduthun', as if it were a dedication; the Hebrew is the plain preposition 'al ('on, upon'), and the commentators split on what it points to. Rashi and Metzudat Zion take Jeduthun as the name of a musical instrument, Radak and Meiri as the Levite singer of David's day who was given the psalm to perform (Meiri reads 'al as 'el, 'to'), and Rashi adds a homiletic reading, 'on the decrees' that were issued against Israel. Jeduthun's family were among the temple singers, so the performing tradition and the man cannot be pulled apart. The attribution 'of David' (ledavid) uses the same lamed that can mean 'by', 'for' or 'belonging to'; the ancient audience would have heard the psalm in David's voice either way.

philological_notes.note: The lamed marks the dedication of the piece to a leader; from a root that means 'to excel, be preeminent', so the participle is the one who presides over the choir. The KJV's 'chief Musician' is acceptable, though the older sense of 'overseer' (YLT) is closer to the root.
Either an instrument, a tune, or the Levite Jeduthun; Rashi and Metzudat Zion say an instrument, Radak and Meiri the man.

verses.translation_literal: Only toward God [is] silence, my soul; from him [is] my salvation.
verses.translation_dramatic: Only toward God does my soul grow quiet. The whole world may shout; my rescue comes from him, and from no other.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm opens with its key word, 'akh ('only, surely, nothing but'), and it will return five more times, six in all, at the head of verses 3, 5, 6, 7 and 10. Play it like a hammer, never loud. The KJV's 'Truly my soul waiteth upon God' turns the opening into a mild affirmation and turns the silence into waiting. The Hebrew says 'silence' (dumiyah), a noun: my soul is silence, toward God. ASV 'waiteth in silence' is closer. Rashi glosses it as 'hoping', and Metzudat Zion as 'hope', but the root is the same as 'be still, be struck dumb' (compare Psalm 37:7, which Rashi cites). Here the stillness is not passivity. It is the opposite of the noise of the plotters in verse 5, who speak blessings with the mouth and curse inside. The 'soul' (nefesh) is the whole living self, throat and breath, not a ghost inside. The speaker is under threat: salvation (yeshu'ah) in Hebrew is concrete rescue from enemies, not an abstract state of being saved.

philological_notes.note: 'Only, surely, nothing but'; the psalm's refrain. Radak reads it as exclusion: do not hope in another god, for my salvation comes only from him. KJV 'Truly' keeps the assertion and loses the exclusion.
A noun: silence, stillness. Meiri notes that it is related to the verb dumi in v. 6 and to Psalm 65:2; Rashi reads it as 'hoping'.

verses.translation_literal: Only he [is] my rock and my salvation, my refuge; I will not be shaken much.
verses.translation_dramatic: He alone is my rock, my rescue, my high place. I will stagger, perhaps, but I will not fall.
verses.directors_commentary: Three images in a row, each a place a hunted man can run to. 'Rock' (tzur) is the cliff face of the Judean hills, a place no cavalry can climb; 'refuge' (misgav) is a height, a raised place out of reach, which is why ASV and BBE say 'high tower' and the KJV's 'defence' goes flat. The KJV keeps 'only' but attaches it to 'He' ('He only is my rock'), where the Hebrew opens the line with 'akh, the same hammer as in verse 2. It also half-softens the last clause, 'I shall not be greatly moved'. The Hebrew verb is 'emot (I will totter, slip), what a foot or a wall does, and 'rabbah' ('much') is deliberately modest: the speaker admits that he will wobble but says he will not fall. Rashi's midrash hears a pun on 'great', with 'Gehenna the great' as the abyss he will not fall into. Ibn Ezra reads the word as the abyss of the deep, 'tehom', which is feminine in Hebrew like 'rabbah'. Whichever way the ancient audience heard it, the image is of a body on a ledge, not a soul in a church.

philological_notes.note: 'My rock': a boulder or cliff, a natural fortress. Meiri glosses it 'my strength'.
From the root 'be high, inaccessible': a refuge because it cannot be reached. 'Defence' (KJV) loses the height.
'Much, greatly'. Radak and Meiri supply an unstated noun, 'a great toppling'; Rashi cites a midrash 'great Gehenna'. It is the word dropped in verse 7.

verses.translation_literal: Until when will you assail a man; will you all be murdered, like a leaning wall, a fence being pushed down?
verses.translation_dramatic: How long, how long will you hurl yourselves at one man, all of you together? You are a leaning wall already, a fence shoved to its fall.
verses.directors_commentary: The voice changes from prayer to confrontation: 'until when' is the question of a man at the end of his patience, and the plural 'you' turns on a crowd. The KJV smooths the verbs into 'imagine mischief' and 'ye shall be slain'. The first verb, tehotetu, is rare, and nobody agrees on it. Rashi gives three readings (a root meaning 'to plot ruin', cf. Psalm 5:10; 'to gather', after Menachem; 'to lengthen your tongue'); the first fits the context best. The second verb, teratzechu, is the plain word for 'murder', not the KJV's 'slain'. It is pointed passively (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri), which makes the line a curse: may you all be murdered. The Ben Naphtali reading with patah would make it active, 'you all murder'. The image that closes the verse is of a mudbrick wall bulging and a loose stone fence under it, both about to fall on whoever stands below. Rashi says it falls on others; Malbim reads the mob as the fence pushed by Saul, the leaning wall, onto David; Radak says that they will live in fear until the end. Note the contrast of the singular 'a man' ('ish) with the 'all of you', the mob against the one.

philological_notes.note: A rare verb; most likely from hawwot, 'ruin, destruction', so 'to plot ruin against'. Rashi also cites Menachem's alternative, 'gather', and a third reading 'lengthen the tongue'.
'Murder' (the verb of the sixth commandment). The qamets pointing makes it a passive, which is why Radak and Meiri hear a curse; the Ben Naphtali reading has patah, which would make it active.
A leaning wall: a standard picture of imminent collapse. Rashi says it is the wall that falls on people.

verses.translation_literal: Only from his height they have counseled to thrust [him] down; they are pleased with a lie; with his mouth they bless, and in their inward part they curse. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: They have met, and the only business is to topple him from his height. They love a lie. The mouth says blessing; the heart, down where no one sees, says curse. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: Here the crowd of verse 4 is drawn from the inside. Their plan has one purpose, to push the man down (lehadiach). The word sounds like the 'pushed-down' fence (hadechuyah) of the last verse, though the two come from different roots; Ibn Ezra points to the link, and the sound alone keeps the image hanging over the plot. The KJV's 'his excellency' is an archaism for what is a plain word, se'et, 'height, rank, dignity' (ASV 'dignity', BBE 'place of honour'): the target is a man who has risen, and the plot is envy. The verb 'they are pleased with a lie' (yirtzu kazav) is more pointed than 'delight in lies': they take pleasure in it, like a banquet. Then the sharp pair: 'with his mouth they bless, in their inward part they curse'. 'Inward part' (qerev) is the guts, the seat of what a person really is, a body word the KJV renders as the faint 'inwardly'. Notice the grammar slides from 'they' to 'his mouth', a singular that Rashi says means each one separately. Each man has the mask. 'Selah' is a mark of uncertain meaning: a rest, a pause or a lifting of the voice. Treat it as the held breath after the accusation.

philological_notes.note: 'From his height, his rank'. The sense is dignity; Radak and Meiri read the suffix as God ('from his loftiness'), while Metzudat David attributes the plot to each plotter's own pride and loftiness.
'To thrust down, drive away'. It echoes in sound the 'pushed-down' fence (hadechuyah) of v. 4, which is from a different root (דחה); Ibn Ezra connects the two.
'A lie', literally something that fails like a dry stream; Metzudat Zion cites Isaiah 58:11, 'whose waters do not fail (yekhazvu)'.
The inward parts, the seat of thought and intention. Rashi paraphrases it as 'in their thoughts'.

verses.translation_literal: Only to God be silent, my soul, for from him [is] my hope.
verses.translation_dramatic: And I, to my own soul, I say: only to God be still. Be still, for every hope I have comes from him.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalmist turns away from the crowd and speaks to himself. The line repeats verse 2, with one difference of grammar that changes the scene: in verse 2 the soul was said to be silence; now it is commanded to be so. The imperative dumi is feminine, because nefesh is a feminine word, and the whole line is a man talking himself down from the ledge, the stillness he states in verse 2 being a thing he must repeat to himself when the crowd is in his ear. The KJV's 'wait thou only upon God' makes it a patient waiting, and the ASV 'wait in silence' adds a little of the right word. The Hebrew has no 'wait'; it says 'be silent', the root of 'silence' in verse 2 and of the Hebrew for 'be struck dumb'. Ibn Ezra and Meiri hear the speaker saying this to himself, while Radak hears an additional 'hope' (hoheli, 'wait for him') in it. 'Hope' (tiqvah) is also the word for a cord, as in Joshua 2:18; there is a rope in it, but I leave that to the reader.

philological_notes.note: Imperative feminine singular, 'be silent, be still', addressed to nafshi, 'my soul'. In v. 2 the same root appears as a noun.
'My hope, my expectation'. The KJV 'expectation' is accurate but archaic.

verses.translation_literal: Only he [is] my rock and my salvation, my refuge; I will not be shaken.
verses.translation_dramatic: He alone is my rock, my rescue, my high place. I will not be shaken. Not at all.
verses.directors_commentary: The same line as verse 3, with one word gone. 'Much' (rabbah) has dropped out, and the clause now ends flat: 'I will not be shaken', with nothing left to qualify it. That is the thing to play. In verse 3 the speaker admitted that he might wobble; now, with his soul quiet, the wobble is gone. Radak says that the omission is the point, a stronger trust than before. The KJV and ASV keep the difference ('greatly moved' in verse 3, 'moved' here); the BBE is the version that loses it, giving 'I will not be greatly moved' in both verses. Hebrew refrain works by small changes, and the loss of one word is the whole step from fear to calm. The sounds help: 'tzuri, yeshu'ati, misgavi', three words each ending in -i, 'my', hammer the possessive, a man counting on his fingers all he owns.

philological_notes.note: 'I will not be shaken'. Compared with v. 3, the adverb rabbah is gone. Radak explains it as the stronger confidence of the one who looks to his deliverance.

verses.translation_literal: On God [is] my salvation and my glory; the rock of my strength, my shelter, [is] in God.
verses.translation_dramatic: My rescue rests on God, and so does my honor. The rock that is my strength, the shelter I run to, is in God.
verses.directors_commentary: The vocabulary of the last verses is now stacked: salvation, glory, rock, strength, shelter. 'Glory' (kavod) is literally 'weight', the heaviness of a reputation that counts, and it is the thing the plotters of verse 5 want to knock down. The verse is built as a chiasm, with God at the beginning and the end. The Hebrew uses two different prepositions: the first half is 'al, 'upon God', as a load rests on a beam, and the second is be-, 'in God', as a man is in a fortress; the KJV's 'In God ... in God' flattens them into one. Metzudat David hears the first half as a promise (God has pledged him the kingship, and the weight is on God to deliver it), while Malbim sharpens it: the glory is by promise, and the refuge is by character. 'The rock of my strength' is a construct chain: a rock that is the source of strength, not a strong rock. The word for salvation here is yesha', the shorter poetic form of yeshu'ah.

philological_notes.note: 'My glory, my honor', literally the 'weight' of a person's standing. Radak hears it as the honor the nations will give after deliverance; Metzudat David and Malbim as the promised kingship.
'The rock of my strength': a construct chain, the rock that is the source of my strength, not a strong rock.

verses.translation_literal: Trust in him at every time, O people; pour out before him your heart. God [is] a refuge for us. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: Trust him, people, in every hour. Pour your hearts out in front of him, all of it, to the last drop. God is a refuge for us. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: From soliloquy to sermon: the psalmist turns outward and speaks to the congregation, with plural imperatives for the first time. The change of 'my' to 'our' (lanu) in the last clause is the shift the whole psalm has been walking toward. 'At every time' ('et) is concrete: in the good season and the bad, in the exile (Radak), in prosperity (Meiri). The KJV's 'ye people' is accurate but sounds like a pulpit; the Hebrew is a single short word of address, 'am. 'Pour out' (shifku) is the verb used for pouring water, blood and libation (Hannah in 1 Samuel 1:15 pours out her soul in the same way); the heart is emptied as a jug is, which is the opposite of the plotters, who keep the curse in their guts. Malbim lists three reasons it is better to trust God than man: He is not unavailable in a bad hour, you can show Him your whole heart without shame, and He gives refuge rather than mere hope.

philological_notes.note: 'Pour out': the verb of water, blood and libations. Radak and Metzudat David read it as prayer; Radak as full repentance.
'O people', vocative. Targum says the house of Israel; Radak and Meiri say the exiles; Metzudat David 'the sons of my people'.

verses.translation_literal: Only a breath [are] the sons of Adam, a lie the sons of man; in the balances, to go up, they [are] lighter than breath together.
verses.translation_dramatic: And men? Only a breath, the common and the great alike, a lie, a vapor. Set them on the scales and up they go, the pan flying high, lighter than breath, all of them together.
verses.directors_commentary: 'Sons of Adam' and 'sons of ish' are not synonyms. The first is the common run of humankind; the second is men of standing, so ASV 'low degree' and 'high degree' have caught the contrast, though the Hebrew has no words for rank, only these two words for 'man'. The point is a merism: everyone, high and low. The central word is hevel, 'breath, vapor', the word that Ecclesiastes will make famous (the KJV there says 'vanity'); in Hebrew it is literally the puff of breath on a cold morning, which is gone as you watch. Ibn Ezra sees Solomon's 'vanity of vanities' behind it. Then a small joke in the Hebrew: 'in the balances to go up'. In an ancient market the heavier thing sinks and the lighter rises; the speaker sets human beings on one pan and breath on the other, and it is the humans that rise, being lighter. Metzudat David notes this is an inverted way of saying 'together they are less than breath'. The KJV 'to be laid in the balance' loses the climbing motion, and so loses the joke.

philological_notes.note: 'Breath, vapor': the wisp that vanishes. The KJV 'vanity' is a Latin-derived word (vanitas) that has drifted from this physical picture.
'In the balances, to go up': the lighter pan rises, so the humans are lighter than breath. Metzudat David reads it as a reversed saying; Rashi adds that the midrash links it to pairs.

verses.translation_literal: Do not trust in extortion, and in robbery do not become breath; wealth, if it bears fruit, do not set [your] heart.
verses.translation_dramatic: Don't lean on extortion. Don't breathe yourselves thin on plunder. And if wealth should sprout and swell, don't give it your heart.
verses.directors_commentary: From the weakness of people to the weakness of what they trust. Two crimes are named, and they are different: 'oshek is the extortion or withholding of what is owed (Radak: money that came into your hand and you will not return it), gazel is taking by force. Ibn Ezra says by deceit and by force. The KJV's 'oppression' and 'robbery' are close, but the first is a legal word, 'oshek, the wrong of the employer who keeps the wages. Then the echo: 'do not become breath' (tehbalu) is the verb made from the noun hevel of the last verse, which the KJV's 'become not vain' loses entirely; a man who trusts in loot makes himself the vapor he has just been told people are. The last clause, 'if wealth bears fruit', uses a verb (yanuv) taken from the word for a harvest, as Rashi, Ibn Ezra, and Metzudat Zion note, and it speaks of money as a crop. The Hebrew is blunt about the heart: 'do not set heart', without 'upon them', an object the KJV adds in italics. Chayil is also army, strength; here it means wealth.

philological_notes.note: A denominative verb from hevel: 'do not make yourselves breath, do not become empty'. The echo with v. 10 is the point.
Extortion, wrongful withholding; distinguished by Radak from gazel, forcible seizure.
'Bears fruit, sprouts', from the root of tenuvah, 'produce, crop'. Rashi cites Isaiah 27:6.

verses.translation_literal: One [thing] God has spoken; two [things] I have heard this: that strength [belongs] to God.
verses.translation_dramatic: God has spoken once, and I have heard it twice over, and this is what it said: strength belongs to God.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm now reaches its summit with a formula the ancient listener knew from wisdom poetry, the numerical saying 'one thing ... two things': the speaker announces a count, and the audience waits for what comes. The KJV 'God hath spoken once; twice have I heard this' hides the arithmetic. The Hebrew sets 'one' beside 'two' (the feminine forms agree with an unnamed 'thing' or 'word'), and each tradition resolves it differently. Rashi, Metzudat David and Malbim hear one divine word and two lessons drawn from it, the second of which comes in the next verse ('and yours, LORD, is loving-kindness'); Radak and Ibn Ezra take 'once, twice' as 'many times', a settled teaching. The text itself names only one fact: 'strength' ('oz) belongs to God, the same word as 'my strength' in verse 8, so the psalm's argument comes full circle. The point for the actors is the contrast: the plotters hold a plan, the rich hold wealth, but 'oz, power in the plain sense of force, is not theirs. Rashi adds that the hearing is as at Sinai, from the second commandment.

philological_notes.note: A numerical saying: 'one ... two'. Rashi and Malbim count one utterance with two lessons; Radak and Ibn Ezra read 'many times'.
'Strength, power', the same word as 'my strength' in v. 8 (the rock of my strength). KJV 'power' is acceptable, though it loses the link.

verses.translation_literal: And to you, Lord, [belongs] steadfast love, for you, you repay to a man according to his deed.
verses.translation_dramatic: And yours, Lord, is the steadfast love, the loyalty that does not let go. For you, and no other, give back to every human being as his own deeds have earned.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends on two short lines that sit close together, with no connecting word of comfort between them. The first line, 'to you, Lord, steadfast love', puts the pronoun first: this answers the power just named in verse 12, where God is strong, and the two things said to belong to God (strength and loyalty) are the two things a worshipper under pressure needs from a judge. Play it as an act of trust, a man laying his case down, not a closing platitude.

The second line is the point where commentators stop to argue. A modern ear hears 'repay according to his deed' as a threat, and the KJV's 'renderest' (an archaism for 'give back') only deepens that sound. But the Hebrew verb is שִׁלֵּם, from the root that gives shalom: it means to make whole, to settle an account so that nothing is outstanding. The ancient listener, living in a world where a patron or a king paid back loyalty and betrayal in kind, heard that as a guarantee that the account would be closed, and that the powerful whom the psalmist has been fearing would not escape it. The KJV also makes 'every man' of לְאִישׁ, which is simply 'to a man'; the 'every' is its own addition, though the sense is fair. The Hebrew keeps the word 'deed' (מַעֲשֶׂה) concrete: work done, not an abstract 'reward' as the BBE has it, which turns the sentence into payment and loses the repayment of what was actually done.

Why the two lines belong together is the question the commentators answer differently. Rashi reads the repayment itself as loyalty: God repays less than the deed deserves. Metzudat David finds the loyalty in the fit of the punishment to the offense, which teaches the sinner to see the hand behind it and return. Radak and Ibn Ezra offer a harder reading, with 'for' as 'although', so that loyalty wins out even though God repays. The plain reading is simplest: God is loyal, and for that reason God's recompense can be trusted.

philological_notes.note: STEPBible glosses it 'covenant loyalty': loyalty owed and given inside a relationship, and acted on, not merely felt. 'Mercy' (KJV) captures only the part that spares; here it also means the faithfulness on which the repayment in the next line rests. Rashi makes the loyalty the very repayment, God paying less than the deed deserves.

Piel of the root 'be complete, whole', so 'make good, pay in full, requite' (STEPBible: 'you repay'). The root sense is my own reading; it is why the verse can sit beside 'steadfast love' without contradiction.
'According to his deed': the thing done, singular and concrete, with the third-person suffix pointing back to 'a man'.
